extracted.intended_audience: grant writers and nonprofit organisations (organizations) seeking foundation or program funding
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing competitive grant proposals: diagnosing common causes of rejection and concrete fixes for alignment, needs assessment, objectives, budgets, evaluation, sustainability, compliance, and differentiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of Alignment with Funder Priorities and Guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: A fundamental mismatch where the proposal fails to directly address the funder's stated priorities, mission, and specific guidelines; submitting generic 'one-size-fits-all' proposals signals lack of targeted research and leads to quick rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deconstruct the RFP by highlighting keywords, priority areas, and required outcomes; create a compliance matrix mapping funder priorities to your project elements; mirror funder language where appropriate to show you've done homework. Example anti-pattern: proposing a senior-citizen arts program to a K-12 STEM funder. Tool tip: use RFP-analyzers to extract priorities, eligibility, and evaluation criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weak or Unclear Problem Statement and Needs Assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposal that does not convincingly establish why the work is necessary — lacking compelling data, credible evidence, or a clear sense of urgency — prevents reviewers from understanding scope or significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate mixed data (quantitative stats and qualitative testimonials); prioritize local and current sources (municipal reports, school district data, recent studies); explain the 'so what' by connecting statistics to real-world consequences. Avoid vague or outdated claims (e.g., relying on decade-old census data). Use tools or templates to weave data into a persuasive narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of Clear, Measurable Goals and Objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Describing aspirational visions rather than concrete plans — vague objectives (e.g., 'improve community health') give funders no way to evaluate success and suggest a lack of operational clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate goals into SMART objectives (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound); establish baseline data; define what will be measured, how, when, and who is responsible; balance quantitative metrics with qualitative stories. Example: change 'provide job training' to 'Train 75 unemployed adults in healthcare certifications, with 70% achieving employment within 6 months at wages above $18/hour.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Insufficient or Unconvincing Evidence of Organizational Capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to demonstrate financial stability, qualified staff, appropriate infrastructure, or a track record to execute the proposed project leads funders to view the request as high-risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight key personnel with relevant bios and experience; showcase past program results with quantified impact; document systems for financial management, M&E, and quality assurance (note recent independent audits if available); use partnerships, advisory boards, or consultants to fill capacity gaps. Provide concrete examples (budgets, org charts, past outcomes) to build credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Missing or Inadequate Project Budget and Budget Justification
rubrics_metrics.description: A vague, unrealistic, or misaligned budget undermines the narrative; unclear line items or insufficient justification raise questions about planning and fiscal responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Itemize all expenses (break broad categories into specific line items); show calculations for each cost (e.g., salary, FTE, months); ensure consistency between the narrative and budget (project activities must match budgeted resources). Include budget justifications that explain how costs were estimated. Use structured budget templates and cross-reference tools to flag inconsistencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poor Writing Quality, Organization, and Presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Poorly written, disorganized, or visually unappealing proposals — grammar errors, jargon, undefined acronyms, inconsistent formatting — reduce readability and signal lack of professionalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create a master outline that follows the funder's required sections; write in clear active voice and keep sentences concise; define acronyms on first use; proofread (read aloud) and obtain multiple reviewers; standardize formatting (single professional font, consistent headings, one-inch margins) and use white space and bullet points to improve scannability. Avoid excessive jargon and inconsistent terminology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to Address Evaluation and Impact Measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Not articulating how success will be measured or failing to present a credible evaluation plan signals lack of accountability; vague promises to 'track progress' are insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop a logic model linking inputs, activities, outputs, and outcomes; define SMART metrics for each outcome (what, how, when, why); budget 5–10% (or appropriate portion) of project funds for evaluation activities (staff time, software, external evaluators); provide validated instruments and data collection schedules. Give concrete examples (e.g., DIBELS administered pre/post with target % change).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inadequate or Missing Sustainability Plan
rubrics_metrics.description: Lacking a credible plan for continuing the project after grant funds end makes the project appear short-term and risky; vague statements like 'we will seek other funding' are insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outline 2–3 specific sustainability streams (earned income, diversified funders, integration into core budget); secure partner commitments with MOUs or letters detailing future contributions; develop a post-grant budget projecting first-year costs and funding sources for each expense. Model multi-year financial scenarios to show feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance, Submission Requirements, and Letters of Support (Format, Attachments, and Endorsements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Careless compliance errors (exceeding page limits, wrong file formats, missing signatures) or weak/generic letters of support can cause automatic disqualification or reduce credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create a detailed submission checklist from the RFP (page limits, font size, margins, required attachments, signatures); provide guidance templates to letter-writers (one-page overview, outcomes to highlight, deadlines); collect diverse external endorsements (beneficiaries, partners, officials) and prefer specific impact evidence over generic praise; assign a compliance checker for final review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inability to Demonstrate Competitive Advantage or Differentiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Failing to articulate what makes the approach unique or more effective causes proposals to blend with many similar applicants; reviewers need reasons to pick your project over others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify 2–3 core differentiators (superior outcomes, evidence-based model, unique partnerships, lived experience of staff); use comparative data to prove advantage (compare outcomes to local/state/national averages); tell an authentic story showing why your organization is best placed to deliver. Conduct funder-specific past-award analysis to position your proposal in the competitive landscape.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision in Alignment and Planning (Key Takeaway Pillar)
rubrics_metrics.description: The most common mistake is misalignment with funder priorities — proposals must be precisely tailored to the funder's history, mission, and RFP specifics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before writing, dissect the RFP; use checklists to verify every guideline (including technical requirements like font and attachment naming); ensure every narrative element maps to a funder priority. Treat alignment and planning as foundational to every other section.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity in Narrative and Impact (Key Takeaway Pillar)
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposal must be a clear, compelling story: articulate the urgent problem, present a concrete solution with measurable objectives, and avoid jargon and assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use SMART objectives, strong needs assessment, and clear evaluation plans; make narrative readable and scannable; integrate both quantitative metrics and qualitative stories to demonstrate impact. Ensure consistency of terminology and logic across sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credibility in Capacity and Finances (Key Takeaway Pillar)
rubrics_metrics.description: Funders invest in organizations they trust; credibility is shown through transparent budgets, documented organizational capacity, and realistic sustainability planning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support claims with staff bios, audited financials, past program data, itemized budgets with justifications, and formal partner commitments. Every number and capability claim should be backed by evidence to reduce perceived delivery risk.
